strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: how to tokenize 3D molecules for AR generation while respecting SE(3) and permutation symmetry, with a clean two-step solution (inertial frame alignment + canonical graph-based atom reordering).

Theorem 1 (and its detailed proof in the appendix) gives a principled, non-trivial argument for why a fourth anchor point is necessary and sufficient to resolve the reflection ambiguity of inertial frames, which is a nice piece of rigor often missing in similar canonicalization schemes.

GeoRoPE is a reasonably elegant way to inject both relative positional information (via a 3D extension of RoPE) and pairwise-distance information (via a Nyström low-rank RBF approximation) into standard dot-product attention without departing from the vanilla Transformer architecture used in large-scale LLMs, which is practically appealing for scaling.
The hierarchical type-then-coordinate prediction with diffusion loss is a sensible adaptation of continuous-token AR modeling (building on Li et al. 2024a) to the atom-based token setting.

Broad empirical evaluation across three datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and a new large-scale B3LYP benchmark) plus a novel and practically relevant class-conditional/functional-group-controlled generation task with a custom Hit Rate metric, showing large improvements in controllability over EDM and Geo2Seq.
Extensive appendices provide self-contained background (RoPE, Nyström method, quaternions/rotations) that aids reproducibility of the mathematical machinery.
weaknesses: No ablation study is presented for the two central architectural claims: the paper asserts that RoPE-3D alone is insufficient and that Nyström pairwise-distance encoding is needed ("We empirically observe..."), but no quantitative ablation (e.g., RoPE-3D only vs. +Nyström, with/without canonical reordering, with/without diffusion loss) is shown to substantiate this design choice.

The unconditional generation results are mixed rather than uniformly state-of-the-art: on QM9, MiDi outperforms InertialAR on Valid and Valid&Uniqueness, and on GEOM-Drugs GeoLDM has higher Valid; the abstract's framing ("7 of 10 metrics") somewhat overstates a picture that is more nuanced in Table 1, and some baseline entries are missing (e.g., Uniqueness on GEOM-Drugs).

A highly relevant and seemingly very similar concurrent work, Cheng et al. 2025b ("Scalable autoregressive 3D molecule generation", also atom-based AR with diffusion loss), is cited in related work but never empirically compared against, despite apparent architectural overlap (hierarchical AR + diffusion loss for coordinates). This omission makes it hard to assess the paper's true incremental novelty and competitiveness.

One of the central motivating claims for using AR over diffusion models is inference efficiency and flexible variable-length generation, but no runtime/throughput/sampling-speed comparisons are provided anywhere in the paper to substantiate this claimed advantage.

The class-conditional benchmark and functional-group labeling pipeline are newly constructed by the authors (custom QM9 relabeling with SMARTS matching), and it is unclear whether baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) were adequately adapted/tuned for this specific conditioning setup, raising some concern about the fairness of the very large reported gains in Hit Rate.

Evaluation relies primarily on atom/molecule stability and validity, without additional standard 3D-generation quality metrics (e.g., bond length/angle distributions, FCD, or comparisons to ground-truth conformer geometry), limiting insight into geometric fidelity beyond basic chemical valence rules.

Details on computational cost, model size, and training budget for the large-scale B3LYP experiments (only a 1M-molecule subset of an 86M dataset is used) are sparse, and no code/data release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility.

strengths: Tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: canonical, SE(3)- and permutation-invariant tokenization of 3D molecules for autoregressive Transformer modeling.

The treatment of inertial-frame sign/direction ambiguity via a fourth anchor node is handled with a formal uniqueness proof (Theorem 1/2), going beyond the usual heuristic PCA-sign-fixing used in prior inertial-frame work (e.g., AssembleFlow, Cheng et al. 2025a).

GeoRoPE is a reasonably elegant architectural idea: it decomposes the attention score into an interpretable sum of a RoPE-3D relative-position term and a Nyström-approximated RBF pairwise-distance term (Eq. 14), integrating geometric information into standard dot-product attention without architectural surgery.

Fairly broad empirical scope: unconditional generation on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs, a new large-scale B3LYP benchmark, and a custom class-conditional/functional-group controllable generation benchmark with CFG-based molecule editing.
Extensive appendix with derivations (Nyström approximation, RoPE matrix-exponential form, quaternion/complex-number background) that aids reproducibility of the mathematical machinery.
weaknesses: No ablation studies isolating the contributions of the paper's main proposed components (inertial-frame canonicalization vs. alternative frames, WL-based atom reordering vs. random/other orderings, RoPE-3D alone vs. + Nyström term, hierarchical type-then-coordinate factorization vs. alternatives). With three simultaneous novel components, it is impossible to assess which actually drives the reported gains.

The headline claim of 'state-of-the-art on 7/10 metrics' is inflated: on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs (Table 1) InertialAR wins only 3 of 6 metrics, losing Validity and Uniqueness-related metrics to MiDi/GeoLDM/UniGEM; GEOM-Drugs Molecule Stability is not even reported, which is suspicious given it is a standard metric in all cited baselines' own papers.

The B3LYP large-scale comparison (Table 2), which contributes 4 of the 7 claimed 'SOTA' metrics, only benchmarks against two relatively weak baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) and omits stronger competitors (GeoLDM, UniGEM, MiDi) citing computational cost, undermining the significance of this result.

No analysis of training/inference wall-clock time or sampling efficiency, despite the introduction motivating AR models specifically via their claimed efficiency advantage over iterative diffusion sampling — this central motivating claim is never empirically substantiated.
No variance/multiple-seed reporting for any table, making it hard to judge whether the (often small) margins over strong baselines such as GeoLDM/UniGEM on QM9 are statistically meaningful.

The inertial-frame construction relies on eigen-decomposition of the inertia tensor and a 'largest-distance' 4th anchor atom; near-degenerate eigenvalue cases (common for molecules with partial symmetry, not just exact symmetry like CO2/CH4) could cause discontinuous/unstable canonical frames, but this robustness issue is not empirically investigated (e.g., sensitivity to small coordinate perturbations).

The canonical atom-reordering step uses purely graph/topological (WL-style) refinement via RDKit, decoupled from the 3D geometry; it is unclear how this interacts with the inertial frame and whether it introduces train/generation distribution mismatches, and no justification or ablation for this choice over alternatives is given.

The class-conditional benchmark (functional-group Class IDs) is a custom construction by the authors with a bespoke SMARTS-based labeling pipeline; details of its validation, bias, and class balance are not reported, and comparisons are only against 2 baselines, limiting confidence in the 'SOTA on all 5 metrics' claim.

Limitations are not explicitly discussed in the main text (the 'Future Directions' paragraph is aspirational, not a critical limitations discussion), leaving open questions about scalability to larger/more flexible molecules, dependence on RDKit canonicalization, and failure modes unaddressed.

No code/data release is mentioned, and several implementation details (e.g., number of Nyström anchor points, kernel bandwidth σ, network sizes, training budgets) are not specified in the main text, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: adapting autoregressive Transformers to 3D molecule generation, with two principled contributions (canonical tokenization via inertial frames + permutation-invariant reordering, and GeoRoPE for geometry-aware attention).

The inertial-frame tokenization is backed by a rigorous theoretical argument (Theorem 1/2 with proof in the appendix) showing why a fourth, non-coplanar reference point is necessary and sufficient to resolve the sign ambiguity of the principal axes, which is a nice piece of geometric reasoning rarely seen in this literature.

GeoRoPE is an elegant combination of RoPE-3D (for relative positional awareness) and a Nyström-based encoding (for pairwise distance), and the derivation showing that the resulting attention score additively decomposes into a relative-position term and an RBF pairwise-distance term (Eq. 14) is clean and interpretable, while remaining compatible with standard Transformer attention (unlike prior distance-injection schemes).

The hierarchical AR factorization (atom type via cross-entropy, then coordinates via diffusion loss) is a sensible design choice that cleanly separates discrete and continuous prediction, drawing on existing diffusion-loss literature but applying it coherently to the 3D molecule setting.

Experiments span three datasets of increasing scale and complexity (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and a newly introduced large-scale B3LYP benchmark with 1M molecules), and the method shows consistent and in some cases dramatic improvements (e.g., Molecule Stability 24.2% vs. 0.8% for EDM on B3LYP), suggesting good scalability.

The paper introduces a novel and useful class-conditional benchmark based on functional-group configurations with a new Hit-Rate metric, together with CFG-based molecule editing visualization, extending the evaluation beyond simple unconditional generation toward practically relevant controllable generation.
weaknesses: No ablation study isolating the contributions of the three main components (inertial-frame tokenization, RoPE-3D, Nyström distance encoding, hierarchical vs. joint prediction); it is therefore unclear which design choice drives the reported gains, weakening the causal story connecting the proposed mechanisms to the empirical improvements.

The unconditional results are mixed rather than uniformly superior: on QM9, MiDi beats InertialAR on Valid and Valid&Uni, and UniGEM matches/exceeds on AtomSta; on GEOM-Drugs, GeoLDM/UniGEM win on Valid, and MolSta for GEOM-Drugs is not even reported in Table 1. The abstract's framing ("7 of 10 metrics") glosses over this incompleteness.

On the new B3LYP benchmark, only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) are compared, justified by computational cost; this limits the strength of the state-of-the-art claim on this dataset and leaves open whether more competitive diffusion/AR baselines (e.g., GeoLDM, UniGEM, MiDi) would close the gap.

Edge cases for the inertial-frame construction are insufficiently discussed: degenerate eigenvalues (symmetric molecules) and the selection of a unique 4th anchor atom (nearly planar molecules, ties in "largest distance") could create discontinuities or ambiguity in the canonical pose that are asserted but not empirically verified to be harmless.

The RoPE-3D formulation in Eq. (6) appears to use a single frequency θ0 shared across axes/dimensions rather than the multi-frequency scheme standard in RoPE used for expressive relative encoding across many feature dimensions; this is not clearly explained, raising concerns about the expressiveness of the encoding across the full hidden dimension.

The class-conditional benchmark and Hit-Rate metric are introduced by the authors themselves, and the baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) are evaluated with only a direct CFG retrofit rather than any additional tuning for this new task, raising questions about the fairness of the comparison.

Key reproducibility details (model sizes, training compute/time, number of diffusion denoising steps at inference, hyperparameters for CFG scale selection, wall-clock/inference speed comparisons against diffusion baselines) are not clearly presented in the main text, despite efficiency being one of the core motivations for using AR over diffusion models.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated open problem (canonical tokenization for AR 3D molecule generation) and proposes a coherent pipeline addressing both the tokenization (SE(3) + permutation invariance) and architecture (hybrid discrete/continuous token) challenges simultaneously.

GeoPE is a technically interesting contribution: it extends RoPE-style relative positional encoding to continuous 3D coordinates (ManhattanPE) and combines it with a Nyström-based low-rank RBF approximation (EuclideanPE) that is compatible with standard Transformer attention without architectural modification (Eq. 5-15). The derivation showing the attention score decomposes into Manhattan and Euclidean relative-geometry terms is a nice piece of formal reasoning.

The paper includes a rigorous formal treatment (Theorem D.1 and proof) of the sign-disambiguation problem for inertial frames via a fourth anchor point, which is a genuine and non-trivial technical detail often glossed over in prior inertial-frame-based canonicalization work.

Empirical results are reasonably comprehensive: unconditional generation on QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and a large-scale (1M-molecule subset) B3LYP dataset show consistent, often state-of-the-art performance, and the class-conditional/CFG-based generation results show large, consistent margins in Hit Rate and validity over strong baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq).

The paper includes an honest discussion of theoretical limitations of inertial-frame canonicalization (degenerate eigenvalues, axis-flip discontinuities) accompanied by empirical quantification (frequency of degeneracy, perturbation sensitivity) rather than hiding these caveats.
Ablations on Diffusion Loss vs. L2 regression and canonical vs. non-canonical atom ordering support two of the paper's central design choices with clear, large effect sizes.
weaknesses: Claimed novelty is somewhat overstated: inertial-frame canonicalization is explicitly acknowledged in the paper's own related work (Guo et al. 2025; Cheng et al. 2025a; Lu et al. 2025a) as pre-existing in molecular modeling; the contribution is narrowly the application to AR tokenization plus atom reordering via RDKit, which is a comparatively incremental combination of known techniques (inertial frames + RoPE-style rotary encoding + Nyström RBF + MAR's Diffusion Loss).

No ablation isolates the individual contributions of ManhattanPE vs. EuclideanPE within GeoPE — despite GeoPE being one of the three headline contributions, only the coordinate-loss and reordering ablations are provided (Section E.2–E.3), leaving the marginal value of each PE component unverified.

A central motivating claim for AR over diffusion models is sampling efficiency/flexibility (Abstract, Intro), yet no wall-clock or throughput comparison between InertialAR and diffusion baselines (e.g., EDM, GeoLDM) is provided anywhere in the main text or appendix.

On the large-scale B3LYP benchmark, only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) are compared, explicitly due to computational cost; stronger and more recent baselines (GeoLDM, UniGEM, or other AR/voxel-based competitors mentioned in related work) are omitted, weakening the strength of the 'state-of-the-art at scale' claim.

The class-conditional generation benchmark (Molecule Class IDs) is a dataset construction designed entirely by the authors using their own SMARTS/Pattern-to-ID pipeline, with no external validation or use of an established benchmark; this raises some concern about potential circularity or benchmark-specific tuning, and no diversity/novelty analysis (relative to training data) is reported to rule out memorization effects.

The main tables do not report variance/error bars over multiple seeds or sampling runs, making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements (e.g., 92.5 vs 93.2 Valid&Uni, where InertialAR is not best) are statistically meaningful.

The paper explicitly notes that ablation experiments used a 'slightly different experimental configuration' than the main results without specifying what changed, which is a minor reproducibility concern.

RDKit canonical SMILES-based atom reordering ties the method's permutation-invariance guarantee to small organic molecules with well-defined valence/ring structures; applicability to larger, more complex systems (proteins, materials, as suggested in future work) is unclear and untested.

strengths: The combination of inertial-frame canonicalization with RDKit-based deterministic atom reordering to produce a unique, SE(3)- and permutation-invariant atom-level sequence is a reasonably clean and well-motivated tokenization strategy for AR 3D molecule generation.

GeoPE is a technically interesting positional encoding that combines a RoPE-style 'ManhattanPE' (with a clean derivation showing the attention inner product depends only on relative coordinates) with a Nystrom-approximated RBF 'EuclideanPE' for pairwise distance awareness, and the authors provide a full derivation of how these combine in the attention score.

A formal theorem (with proof in Appendix D) justifying why a fourth anchor point is necessary and sufficient to resolve the sign ambiguity of the inertial frame axes is a nice piece of rigor often missing in canonicalization-based molecule generation papers.

The experimental scope is broad: unconditional generation on QM9/GEOM-Drugs, a large-scale B3LYP benchmark, and class-conditional generation/molecule editing with CFG, along with targeted ablations on the diffusion-loss choice, atom reordering, and empirical robustness of the inertial frame under perturbation and degeneracy.

The empirical robustness analysis of the inertial frame (perturbation sensitivity of axis-sign flips, frequency of principal-moment degeneracy) directly and honestly addresses a known theoretical weakness of PCA/inertial-frame canonicalization rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The paper omits comparison to the most directly relevant concurrent work it cites, 'Scalable autoregressive 3D molecule generation' (Cheng et al., 2025b), which addresses essentially the same problem (atom-based AR 3D generation) -- this is a significant gap given the paper's SOTA claims, since the closest competitor is never empirically benchmarked.

The claimed 'SOTA on 8/10 metrics' is misleading on inspection: in Table 1, GeoLDM and UniGEM actually beat InertialAR on QM9 Valid&Uni and GEOM-Drugs Valid, and InertialAR is not uniformly dominant; the gains over the strongest baselines are often small (e.g., 97.3 vs 97.1 Valid on QM9), with no error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results reported to support that these differences are meaningful.

The B3LYP large-scale evaluation is restricted to only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) on a 1M-molecule subset of an 86M-molecule dataset, with no equivariant GNN baselines included; absolute MolSta values remain very low (≤24.7%), undermining the strength of the 'SOTA on all 4 metrics' claim for this dataset.

A central motivating claim of the paper is that AR models are more efficient than diffusion due to avoiding iterative sampling, yet no inference-time, throughput, or wall-clock comparison against diffusion baselines (EDM, GeoLDM, MiDi) is provided anywhere in the paper to substantiate this claimed advantage.

The class-conditional generation benchmark (Molecule Class IDs from functional-group SMARTS matching) is entirely self-constructed by the authors with no external validation, and the qualitative molecule-editing results (Figure 4) are limited to three anecdotal examples without any chemist/expert assessment of validity or usefulness.

The hierarchical type-then-coordinate prediction with cross-entropy + Diffusion Loss is a direct adaptation of MAR (Li et al., 2024a) from image generation to atoms, and the architectural novelty beyond this adaptation plus GeoPE is relatively incremental.

No comparison to alternative atom-ordering schemes (e.g., spatial/BFS-based orderings as used in some prior AR molecule work) is provided; the ablation only compares 'with' vs. 'without' RDKit canonicalization, leaving open whether the chosen canonical order is actually the best choice for AR generation.

Reproducibility is weakened by the abstract's incomplete code link, lack of reported model sizes/parameter counts, training compute, and the explicit admission that ablation experiments used a 'slightly different experimental configuration' than the main results, making exact comparisons across tables unreliable.

The paper's presentation is heavily padded with appendices that largely restate material already in the main text (e.g., duplicated preliminaries, CFG description, dataset reconstruction) rather than providing additional substantive analysis, which does not strengthen the core technical contribution.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of inertial-frame canonicalization with atom-level autoregressive tokenization to simultaneously address SE(3) and permutation invariance for 3D molecule generation, with a careful theoretical treatment (Theorem D.1 and proof) of the sign-ambiguity problem in PCA/inertial frames.

GeoPE is a technically interesting positional encoding that cleanly decomposes attention scores into a Manhattan/RoPE-style relative term and a Nyström-approximated RBF pairwise-distance term, with explicit derivations showing the resulting attention score has an interpretable geometric meaning (Eq. 15).

The hierarchical AR design (cross-entropy for discrete atom type, Diffusion Loss for continuous coordinates) is sensible given the hybrid nature of atom tokens, and is empirically justified by a strong ablation showing L2 regression collapses performance (Table 6).

Comprehensive experiments spanning QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and a new large-scale B3LYP dataset, plus a novel class-conditional generation benchmark (Molecule Class IDs via functional-group SMARTS matching) and molecule-editing demonstration via CFG, showing strong controllability (hit rate ~83% average vs much lower for baselines).

Appendix includes careful empirical robustness analysis of the inertial frame under coordinate perturbations and principal-moment degeneracy, addressing a known theoretical weakness of PCA-based canonicalization with quantitative evidence that it is negligible in practice.
Additional ablations (effect of canonical atom reordering, diffusion vs. L2 loss) support the architectural choices.
weaknesses: Novelty claims ("first to turn inertial-frame canonicalization into a generation-ready tokenization") are somewhat undercut by closely related concurrent/contemporaneous work cited in the same paper (e.g., Guo et al. 2025 AssembleFlow, Cheng et al. 2025a Stiefel flow matching, Zhou et al. 2026, Ni et al. 2026) that also use inertial/PCA frames for molecular or biomolecular modeling; the precise technical delta from these is not deeply analyzed.

Evaluation is incomplete in places: Table 1 omits Valid&Uni and MolSta for GEOM-Drugs, and GeoLDM actually outperforms InertialAR on GEOM-Drugs Valid (99.3 vs 98.0%), yet the abstract/text claims near-uniform SOTA (8/10 or 4/6 metrics) without fully contextualizing these losses.

On the large-scale B3LYP benchmark, comparison is limited to only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) due to stated computational cost; stronger diffusion baselines (GeoLDM, UniGEM) that perform well on GEOM-Drugs are not evaluated there, weakening the strength of the B3LYP SOTA claim.
The claimed efficiency advantage of AR over diffusion (motivated in the introduction) is never empirically substantiated with runtime/sampling-speed comparisons.

Key reproducibility details are missing from the main text/appendix shown: training hyperparameters, model size, compute budget, number of samples used for evaluation metrics, and the actual code repository link (text says "Code is available at" with no URL/further information).
No variance/error bars are reported for the metrics in Tables 1–3, making it hard to assess whether relatively small differences (e.g., Valid 97.1 vs 97.3 on QM9) are statistically meaningful.

The class-conditional benchmark and Molecule Class ID labeling scheme is newly constructed by the authors; it is unclear how fairly EDM and Geo2Seq (not originally designed for this specific multi-attribute functional-group conditioning) were adapted, raising some concern about comparison fairness.

Atom reordering relies on an RDKit canonical SMILES-based heuristic rather than a principled, generation-oriented ordering criterion; the ablation (Table 7) shows only modest effect, leaving open whether the chosen ordering is actually optimal for AR generation versus alternative orderings.
